messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 65-year-old married man of African descent who works at a large home-improvement retail store on the outskirts of his city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a PCL-5 score of 60, and he arrived at the intake appointment with the measured, deliberate manner of someone who had spent months trying to hold himself together through sheer discipline.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Kwame was at work when a severe tornado struck without adequate warning. The storm tore through the building's roof in a matter of seconds, collapsing a section of shelving in the hardware aisle where he had been restocking inventory. He described the sound — a low, pressurised roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once — and the sudden darkness as the power failed, the air filling with debris and the screaming of colleagues he could not see. He pressed himself against a concrete support pillar for what felt like an eternity, certain he was about to die. When the storm passed, he emerged to find two coworkers seriously injured and the building partially destroyed. He was physically unharmed, but something in him, he said quietly, did not survive that afternoon.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of those minutes inside the store refused to settle into the past. Kwame described it as a film that plays over and over without his permission — the roar, the darkness, the debris — and crucially, when the memory surfaces, it carries no temporal distance. He does not remember the tornado; he is inside it again, his body bracing against the pillar, his heart hammering as though the roof is still coming down. This quality of the memory as present rather than past has become one of his most distressing symptoms, and it feeds directly into his sense of ongoing danger. Because the event feels perpetually current rather than concluded, Kwame has come to believe with quiet certainty that the world is genuinely and permanently dangerous — not that it was dangerous on one terrible afternoon, but that threat is the natural condition of existence. He also believes he has been permanently changed for the worse, that the man who walked into that store before the storm is simply gone.

These convictions shape almost everything about how Kwame now moves through daily life. Believing he must be on guard at all times, he enters every room — including the retail floor where he still works — scanning immediately for exits. He has reorganised his working patterns so that he stations himself near the garden-centre doors at the far end of the store, where he can see an exit at all moments. His manager initially accommodated this, but over recent months colleagues have noticed his reluctance to work in the interior aisles, and he has been passed over for a supervisory role he had been informally promised. When the hypervigilance becomes overwhelming on the shop floor, he distracts himself — counting ceiling tiles, focusing on a customer's list — anything to interrupt the flood of sensation. He also struggles to fall asleep each night, lying awake in the belief that alertness is the only thing standing between him and catastrophe.

The tragedy of Kwame's situation is that none of these strategies provide relief; they deepen the problem. Remaining near exits and scanning constantly keeps his nervous system primed, so that ordinary sounds — a trolley rattling, a door slamming — register as potential signals of disaster and pull the memory forward again, vivid and immediate. And when the memory surges back with that quality of happening right now, it confirms for Kwame everything he already fears: that the danger is real, that he was right to stay alert, that the world cannot be trusted. His maladaptive strategies, intended to protect him, have become evidence that protection is necessary, reinforcing the very appraisals that drive them. His wife has noticed that he no longer sits with his back to the room at family gatherings, and that he leaves restaurants if he cannot see the door. He has not told her the full extent of what he experiences, because he is afraid that describing it will make it worse — or that she will confirm his deepest fear, that he is not the man he was.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when a sudden rainstorm produced a sound on the metal roof that sent him to his knees in the aisle, hands over his head, before he had any conscious awareness of what he was doing. A young colleague helped him up without a word, and the shame of that moment was, he said, the first thing that had felt stronger than the fear. He is not certain therapy can help him. What he most hopes for, in his own careful words, is simply to feel that what happened is over.
